title: Parts unusually developed relative to congeners are highly variable

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Parts unusually developed relative to congeners are highly variable

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A part developed to an extraordinary degree or in an extraordinary manner in one species, compared with the same part in closely allied species, tends to be highly variable within that species; the rule does not apply when the unusual part is shared by a whole group.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: _A part developed in any species in an extraordinary degree or manner, in comparison with the same part in allied species, tends to be highly variable_.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter V, “Laws of Variation”; section “Parts developed in an unusual manner are highly variable: specific characters more variable than generic: secondary sexual characters variable.”. Scope: animals, especially birds, cirripedes and secondary sexual characters; Darwin could not confirm it for plants

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch05-12: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.64

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The association is operationally clear after standardizing traits and has a straightforward refuting result. Public data can test selected animal groups, but not Darwin's broad scope or the stated plant uncertainty.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Quantify how exceptional a species' trait is relative to congeners and relate that value to within-species trait variance, distinguishing species-specific from clade-wide novelty. A positive phylogenetically controlled association supports the rule.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Defining an extraordinary degree across heterogeneous traits requires normalization.

Most comparative trait datasets have too few individuals per species.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.62
analysis feasibility: 0.62
data adequacy: 0.44
operationalizability: 0.82
discriminating power: 0.7

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Outlier status and within-species variance are both computable for birds from a public individual-level morphology table plus a phylogeny. That is a large, clean subset and a weak sample of the rest of animals, and it is thin for the sexual characters named in the scope. Allometry and measurement effort are manageable confounds, so the bird test is informative without covering the full statement.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Using individual measurements, compare within-species coefficients of variation of traits that are extreme relative to congeners with variation in ordinary traits, and repeat the comparison for traits that are unusual for a whole clade. Higher variation only in species-level outliers would confirm the rule; no elevation, or equal elevation when the whole group shares the trait, would refute the two clauses.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Individual measurements are often unsexed and unevenly sampled within species.

AVONET traits are primarily size and shape, not the secondary sexual characters Darwin emphasized.

Cirripedes and most non-bird animals lack a comparable individual-level table.

fields.value:

operationalizability: 0.8
analysis feasibility: 0.68
data existence: 0.62
